title: Administrative data becomes useful when leaders can act on it
overview: This week examines how operational data becomes management information and action. Compare DSS and EIS, follow the Collect → Measure → Interpret → Act framework, interpret a KPI in context, and examine HIM responsibilities for purpose, meaning, quality, trust, and workflow use.
objectives: Explain how decision support systems (DSS) and executive information systems (EIS) support different management needs.
Describe the Collect → Measure → Interpret → Act framework for turning operational data into management action.
Explain how healthcare leaders interpret a KPI in context before changing a workflow.
Describe HIM responsibilities for protecting information purpose, meaning, quality, trust, and workflow use.

concepts.name: Decision support system (DSS)
concepts.definition: Supports analysis of a defined decision or problem. It combines data, models, and context to help people evaluate choices, with more detail, analysis, and what-if exploration.

concepts.name: Executive information system (EIS)
concepts.definition: Presents concise, high-level performance views for senior leaders, including trends, exceptions, and KPIs.

concepts.name: Operational systems
concepts.definition: Systems that create the data that management systems summarize.

concepts.name: Key performance indicator (KPI)
concepts.definition: A performance indicator used to present or measure performance. The framework calls for defining a KPI or performance measure before interpreting trends, exceptions, and context.

concepts.name: Scheduling
concepts.definition: Coordinates resources, staff, rooms, and appointments.

concepts.name: Materials and facilities
concepts.definition: Track supplies, equipment, space, and maintenance.

concepts.name: Collect → Measure → Interpret → Act framework
concepts.definition: A sequence for bringing together operational data, defining a KPI or performance measure, interpreting trends, exceptions, and context, and then changing a workflow, resource plan, or policy.

concepts.name: Information quality and meaning
concepts.definition: Information is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood. Definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping support its meaning and quality.

concepts.name: Access and trust
concepts.definition: Privacy, security, integrity, and auditability are protected through policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities
concepts.definition: HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work by explaining purpose, protecting meaning and quality, protecting trust, and improving workflow.

sections.body: Operational systems create the data that management systems summarize. Administrative systems support different areas of work: scheduling coordinates resources, staff, rooms, and appointments, while materials and facilities systems track supplies, equipment, space, and maintenance. These operational activities produce data that can be measured and presented to support management needs. A management view is useful when its information is connected to its purpose, users, and decisions.
sections.title: Management systems start with operational work

sections.body: A decision support system (DSS) supports analysis of a defined decision or problem. It offers more detail, analysis, and what-if exploration to help people consider options. An executive information system (EIS) presents a concise, high-level view for senior leaders, using indicators, trends, and exceptions to show where performance is strong or weak. The distinction is not simply whether a system displays data: a DSS helps examine options for a particular decision, while an EIS gives leaders a compact view of performance.
sections.title: DSS and EIS answer different management questions

sections.body: The Collect → Measure → Interpret → Act framework organizes the path from operational data to management action. First, bring together operational data. Next, define a KPI or other performance measure so the intended measure is clear. Then interpret trends and exceptions in context. Finally, use that interpretation to consider changing a workflow, resource plan, or policy. The stages keep measurement and interpretation distinct from action: a reported result is not, by itself, an explanation or a decision.
sections.title: Turn operational data into action

sections.body: An executive dashboard may show rising length of stay, but leaders should consider the KPI alongside relevant context before changing a workflow. In the example, that context includes case mix, discharge delays, staffing, bed capacity, data definitions, and time trends. Combining these elements helps leaders interpret what the KPI is showing rather than treating the displayed trend as a complete explanation. For HIM, management information becomes useful when operational data are measured consistently, interpreted in context, and connected to an action.
sections.title: Interpret a KPI in context before changing work

sections.body: HIM professionals connect a system’s purpose to trustworthy information work. They clarify users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; support definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; and check identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. They also support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. Finally, feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction help improve workflow and adoption. These responsibilities frame whether information is fit for its intended use and can be used safely and effectively.
